title: Chapter 4: The Law Student
primary_topics: Chapter 4 covers Art's four-year law course at FEU (1956-1960) -- the educational and physical setting of Pablo Antonio's Arellano Hall and Felipe Mendoza's Science Building (later UNESCO-recognized Art Deco), the Our Lady of Fatima Chapel with its National-Artist art program (Botong Francisco, Maximo Vicente, Napoleon Abueva, Vicente Manansala), and the named professors who taught the law-student who was simultaneously running NUSP.

Dean Jovito R. Salonga as the third great mentor of CJP's life -- after Mrs. Fajardo at Juan Luna and Fr. Nolan at FEU -- the role model 'in my chosen career and, more important, in my life as a whole.' Salonga's Harvard-and-Yale academic distinction (rare combination given the schools' non-recognition of each other's degrees), his demand that 'a law student's business is to study and excel,' and his prediction that Art would be a bar topnotcher.

The roster of legal luminaries: future Senate President Neptali A. Gonzales; future SC justices Edgardo L. Paras and Salvador Esguerra; future Court of Appeals justices Arsenio Solidum, Antonio Lucero, Luis B. Reyes, Angel Mojica, Jose Leuterio; young Ivy League returnees Juan Ponce Enrile, Manuel Montecillo, Reynaldo Alejandro, Augusto Caesar Espiritu -- all teaching the future Chief Justice simultaneously.

Two near-death medical episodes during the law years: the 1958 NUS Naga delegation trip where Art's appendix burst on Mt. Mayon (misdiagnosed as indigestion at St. Mary's Maternity Clinic in Tabaco, Albay, treated with castor oil and morphine), and the appendicitis surgery two weeks later at FEU Hospital under Dr. Ricardo Alfonso who told him 'The Lord must love you' because the rupture's location had spared him -- the moment CJP later traces as the third major near-death deliverance of his early life.

The 1960 bar examinations and CJP's #6 finish despite hospitalization with diarrhea and flu during the first Sunday of the exam, walking through flooded R. Papa Street between FEU Hospital and the University of the East under Dean Salonga's emphatic instruction to persist; bracketed by the death of Patricia 'Agang' Panganiban (tuberculosis, streptomycin shortages) in her Marulas, Polo, Bulacan house that Art, Nardo and Frankie had built with their bare hands.

stances.claim: Dean Jovito R. Salonga is the role model of Art's life -- 'not just a good lawyer who topped the Bar,' but a Harvard-and-Yale lawyer who could combine the two rival ivies' degrees, whose moral courage and 'high-mindedness and love of country' Art aspired to internalize. The chapter positions Salonga as the lineage source of CJP's later jurisprudential identity.
stances.rhetorical_move: mentor-as-lineage thesis; tracing CJP's professional voice to a specific named teacher

stances.claim: FEU's faculty -- Salonga, Gonzales, Paras, Esguerra, the future Court of Appeals justices, the young Ivy League returnees including Enrile -- was substantively first-tier, producing bar topnotchers annually. The Quezon 'best non-sectarian institution' framing was empirically true at the time, not just a marketing line.
stances.rhetorical_move: institutional-rehabilitation thesis; defending FEU's pedigree against the UP-Ateneo presumption

stances.claim: Communism remained a live persuasion through law school: Prof. Primo Tongco continued to make the case ('communism was Christianity,' 'to each according to his need'), and the message 'sounded true' to the poor student. Fr. Nolan's earlier formation and Fr. Sheehy's continuing influence held Art in the Christian frame at the level of conviction, not just affiliation.
stances.rhetorical_move: ongoing-tension framing -- formation as continuing defense against attractive alternatives

stances.claim: Three near-death deliverances by 1958 (war/dysentery in childhood, jeepney fall in boyhood, ruptured appendix in law school) form a pattern that Dr. Alfonso names aloud: 'The Lord must love you.' Art reads this only decades later: 'God had a mission for me and thus delivered me from death.' The chapter argues for cumulative providence as the right interpretive frame.
stances.rhetorical_move: cumulative-deliverance argument; providence as pattern not coincidence

stances.claim: The 1960 bar #6 finish -- under hospitalization, after Agang's death, with Dean Salonga's prediction creating performance anxiety so severe Art got physically sick -- is treated as a victory partly *because of* the disadvantages overcome. Salonga's later 'might have placed first or second if he had not been sick' is positioned as testimony, not consolation.
stances.rhetorical_move: overcoming-as-evidence; the difficulty of the bar finish redeems its number

stances.claim: Architecture and art mattered to Art's formation more than is conventionally noted: the Felipe Mendoza Science Building, Pablo Antonio's Arellano Hall, the Botong/Vicente/Abueva/Manansala-decorated chapel were the visual ecosystem of CJP's law-student years. The biography spends an unusual amount of detail on the buildings and the chapel art -- implicitly arguing that aesthetic ecosystem shapes character.
stances.rhetorical_move: environmental-formation thesis; setting as silent teacher

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 4 covers Art's four-year law course at FEU (1956-1960), framed by Psalm 138:7's 'Though I walk in the midst of trouble, you preserve my life.' The chapter opens with the physical setting: Felipe Mendoza's 1957 Science Building (later UNESCO-recognized in 2005), Pablo Antonio's Arellano Hall housing the Institute of Law (commissioned by Dr. Nicanor Reyes, the FEU founder), and the Our Lady of Fatima Chapel decorated by four National Artists -- Botong Francisco's Stations of the Cross and Crucified Christ, Maximo Vicente's life-sized statues, Napoleon Abueva's fiber-glass *La Pieta* inspired by Michelangelo, and Vicente Manansala's unique blue-mosaic Our Lady of Fatima on the facade. The SCA office sat below the chapel, and Art felt drawn to the chapel even before he had 'gotten his spiritual moorings.' The teachers form a register of named formation: Dr. Alejandro R. Roces (Dean of Arts and Sciences) on the truly educated person; Dr. Teodoro Evangelista (FEU president) on education for the life of the mind; Dean Francisco M. Africa on argumentation and debate; Dr. Benito F. Reyes on philosophy and 'theosophy' (whose preacher-philosopher path Art declined out of filial loyalty to Temi's law wish); Prof. Angelica P. Mendoza on botany; Prof. Rosario P. Melchor on English grammar; Prof. Primo Tongco trying to convert the poor student to Marxism ('communism was Christianity,' 'to each according to his need, from each according to his ability' -- 'sounded true' to Art); and Fr. James Sheehy SSC continuing the Columban influence after Fr. Nolan ('a good Catholic must not only be personally pure but must also lead others to purity'). At the Institute of Law itself, Art's faculty was a roll-call of mid-century legal power: Dean Jovito R. Salonga (the role model -- Harvard MA + Yale JSD, a combination the rival ivies normally didn't permit, later Senate President); Neptali A. Gonzales (also future Senate President); Edgardo L. Paras and Salvador Esguerra (future SC justices); Arsenio Solidum, Antonio Lucero, Luis B. Reyes, Angel Mojica, Jose Leuterio (future Court of Appeals justices); and the young Ivy League returnees Juan Ponce Enrile, Manuel Montecillo, Reynaldo Alejandro, Augusto Caesar Espiritu. Salonga monitored Art's grades 'like a father' and admonished, 'I don't care if you are the president of the Central Student Council of FEU and head of the National Union of Students of the Philippines. Your priority as a law student should be your academics.' Two near-death medical episodes punctuate the law years: in 1958, leading the NUS Naga seminar against communism, Art climbed Mt. Mayon and his appendix burst -- misdiagnosed at St. Mary's Maternity Clinic in Tabaco, Albay (the only available clinic, gendered or not) as indigestion, treated with castor oil and then morphine, he slept 24 hours and was dancing that evening; two weeks later, surgery at FEU Hospital under Dr. Ricardo Alfonso, who told him 'Your appendix ruptured two weeks ago. The Lord must love you,' the rupture's atypical posterior-left location and the surrounding fat tissue having contained the toxins long enough for surgical intervention. He paid only the six-peso student fee he had previously opposed as student leader ('You win, Doctor'). A sophomore-year scholarship loss due to over-extended student-leader time was rescued by Uncle Ben's 150 pesos with strict admonition; the scholarship was recovered the next semester. The Marulas, Polo, Bulacan house Art, his brother Nardo and uncle Frankie built with their bare hands became Agang's last home; she succumbed to tuberculosis during Art's fourth year, Nardo administering streptomycin shots when funds allowed. The chapter culminates in the 1960 bar examinations: hospitalized at FEU Hospital on the first Sunday with severe gastroenteritis and flu, discouraged and ready to quit, Art was reached by Salonga whose hand-shake-longer-than-usual was accompanied by 'Art, take the exam; you will get well.' He walked over flooded R. Papa Street to the University of the East and finished #6 -- Bachelor of Laws cum laude -- with Salonga later writing in the 2007 Foreword to *A Test of Courage* that 'Art might have placed first or second if he had not been sick.' Art dropped the 'Jr.' from his name upon admission to the Bar 'to honor him and his last wish ... so that he would truly live in me.'
